nodes.label: Iran
nodes.full: The Shah's claim to Bahrain, dropped in 1971; the 1981 coup plot by the Iran-linked Islamic Front; and the persistent charge and counter-charge of Iranian direction of the Shiʿi opposition.
nodes.src: background — Louër, 'Transnational Shia Politics' (2008).

nodes.label: Saudi Arabia
nodes.full: The patron next door: the causeway, the shared oil field, the recurring bailouts, and the Peninsula Shield troops that entered Bahrain in March 2011 to end the uprising.
nodes.src: background — the 2011–12 Gulf-union proposal; the 2018 GCC package.

nodes.label: The United States
nodes.full: Home to the Fifth Fleet since 1995 and a major non-NATO ally: the security relationship Washington declined to jeopardise over the 2011 crackdown.
nodes.src: background — NSA Bahrain; the 2002 ally designation.

nodes.label: Israel and the US normalisation push
nodes.full: The partner in the Abraham Accords: Bahrain normalised relations with Israel in September 2020, in step with the UAE and Saudi Arabia.
nodes.src: background — the Abraham Accords Declaration (2020).

nodes.label: The Arab Spring
nodes.full: The 2011 regional wave of uprisings that put Bahrainis into the streets and onto the Pearl Roundabout.
nodes.src: background — added on review.

nodes.label: Emir ʿĪsā ibn Salmān Āl Khalīfa
nodes.full: Led Bahrain to independence on 15 August 1971 after the population rejected the Iranian claim in a UN-supervised process, promulgated the 1973 constitution, and then dissolved its elected parliament in 1975 — nearly three decades of rule by decree under the State Security Law.
nodes.src: the 1970 UN mission on Bahrain; the 1973 constitution and its 1975 dissolution decree.

nodes.label: King Hamad ibn ʿĪsā Āl Khalīfa
nodes.full: Opened with the 2001 National Action Charter and made Bahrain a kingdom in 2002, then oversaw the crushing of the 2011 uprising and the destruction of the political opposition. As of early 2026 he remains king.
nodes.src: the National Action Charter referendum (February 2001); the 2002 constitution; this entry records the position as of early 2026.

nodes.label: Prince Khalīfa ibn Salmān, the fifty-year prime minister
nodes.full: The king's uncle was prime minister from before independence until his death in 2020 — the longest-serving unelected prime minister in the world, and the hardline pole of the ruling family against the reform current around the crown prince.
nodes.src: the obituaries and profiles of Prince Khalīfa; the intra-family divide analysed in the 2011 crisis literature.

nodes.label: Crown Prince Salmān ibn Hamad, prime minister
nodes.full: The Western-educated heir, long the face of a reformist current within the family and the government's negotiator in 2011, took the premiership on his great-uncle's death — consolidating the two offices in the direct line.
nodes.src: the November 2020 appointment; the crown prince's 2011 role in the aborted dialogue.

nodes.label: The 1981 coup plot
nodes.full: The Iranian-linked Islamic Front for the Liberation of Bahrain's plot to seize the government was foiled by the security services — the first sign of the Islamic Republic's reach into Bahrain, and the pretext for a decade of Shiʿi repression.
nodes.src: the 1981 arrests and trials; Laurence Louër, 'Transnational Shia Politics' (2008).

nodes.label: The 1990s Intifada
nodes.full: A broad Shiʿi-led and leftist-supported uprising demanding the restoration of the 1973 constitution and parliament — years of protest, arson and arrests, dozens killed, the leaders including Sheikh ʿAbd al-Amīr al-Jamrī jailed or exiled, ended only by King Hamad's succession.
nodes.src: the contemporary Human Rights Watch reporting; the petitions of 1992 and 1994.

nodes.label: The Pearl Roundabout
nodes.full: A cross-sectarian pro-democracy occupation of the Lulu roundabout in central Manama, met with live fire on 17 February, cleared, reoccupied after the army withdrew, and cleared again — the largest protest movement in Bahrain's history.
nodes.src: the Bahrain Independent Commission of Inquiry (BICI) report (2011); the contemporary reporting.

nodes.label: The Peninsula Shield intervention and the crackdown
nodes.full: Saudi and Emirati troops entered Bahrain under the GCC's Peninsula Shield; martial law followed, the Pearl Monument was demolished, and the crackdown — mass arrests, deaths in custody, the trial of the medics, the razing of some thirty Shiʿi mosques — was documented by the government's own commission of inquiry.
nodes.src: the BICI report (2011); the Peninsula Shield deployment of 14 March 2011.

nodes.label: The destruction of the opposition
nodes.full: The dissolution of al-Wefaq and the leftist Waʿad, the life sentences for the 'Bahrain 13', the jailing of ʿAlī Salmān, Nabeel Rajab and ʿAbd al-Hādī al-Khawāja, the revocation of citizenship from over a thousand people, the 2017 siege of Diraz, and the resumption of executions.
nodes.src: the reporting of the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and Amnesty International (advocacy sources, flagged); the 2016 al-Wefaq dissolution; the January 2017 executions.

nodes.label: The 1973 constitution and its dissolution
nodes.full: An elected National Assembly, and its dissolution by the emir eighteen months later when it resisted the State Security Law — the founding grievance of every subsequent Bahraini opposition movement.
nodes.src: the 1973 constitution; the August 1975 dissolution and the suspension of constitutional life.

nodes.label: The Charter and the 2002 Constitution
nodes.full: The 2001 National Action Charter, approved by 98 percent on the promise of a return to elected government, and the 2002 constitution that instead created a bicameral parliament in which the appointed upper house can always block the elected one.
nodes.src: the National Action Charter (2001); the 2002 constitution; the opposition's 'unilateral' critique.

nodes.label: The security state and the citizenship weapon
nodes.full: The State Security Law and its courts, the Jau prison system, and — after 2011 — the mass revocation of citizenship from more than a thousand people, making statelessness a routine tool of political control.
nodes.src: the State Security Law (repealed 2001, its practices continued); the citizenship-revocation tallies compiled by rights groups (advocacy sources, flagged).

nodes.label: The BICI report
nodes.full: The Bahrain Independent Commission of Inquiry, commissioned by the king and chaired by M. Cherif Bassiouni, documented systematic torture, excessive force and unfair trials — a rare official admission, most of whose recommendations were never implemented.
nodes.src: the Report of the Bahrain Independent Commission of Inquiry (23 November 2011).

nodes.label: The Shiʿi majority under a Sunni dynasty
nodes.full: Bahrain is the only Gulf Arab state with a Shiʿi-majority citizen population ruled by a Sunni minority family — the fact that structures its politics, its security services, its geography of villages and towns, and every one of its crises.
nodes.src: Justin Gengler, 'Group Conflict and Political Mobilization in Bahrain and the Arab Gulf' (2015); the disputed census figures.

nodes.label: The clergy and the movements
nodes.full: The Shiʿi religious establishment — Sheikh ʿĪsā Qāsim, the ʿulamāʾ councils, the maʾtams — and the political societies that grew from it, from the Islamic Front of the 1980s to al-Wefaq; and the state's long effort to control, co-opt or crush them.
nodes.src: Louër, 'Transnational Shia Politics' (2008); the 2016 stripping of Sheikh ʿĪsā Qāsim's citizenship.

nodes.label: The Sunni establishment and the loyalist mobilisation
nodes.full: The state Sunni religious apparatus, the Salafi al-Aṣāla and the Brotherhood-linked al-Minbar blocs in parliament, and — after 2011 — the loyalist counter-movements such as the National Unity Gathering that framed the uprising as a sectarian, Iranian project.
nodes.src: Gengler (2015) on the Sunni counter-mobilisation of 2011.

nodes.label: The Pearling Path and the memory of the sea
nodes.full: The Muharraq pearling sites — the merchant houses, the oyster beds, the last pearling boat — inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 as the record of an economy that the Japanese cultured pearl and then oil destroyed in the 1930s.
nodes.src: the UNESCO inscription of 'Pearling, Testimony of an Island Economy' (2012).

nodes.label: Qalʿat al-Bahrain and the Dilmun past
nodes.full: The tell and fort at the ancient Dilmun capital, a UNESCO site, and the Bahrain National Museum's Dilmun galleries — the deep antiquity on which a small modern state built part of its national identity.
nodes.src: the UNESCO inscription of 'Qalʿat al-Bahrain – Ancient Harbour and Capital of Dilmun' (2005).

nodes.label: The Pearl Monument, built and demolished
nodes.full: The six-sailed concrete monument at the Lulu roundabout, a national symbol that had appeared on the coinage, became the centre of the 2011 protests and was demolished by the government in March 2011 — an act of erasure as political as any arrest.
nodes.src: the demolition of 18 March 2011; the withdrawal of the half-dinar coin bearing the monument.

nodes.label: The fidjeri and Bahraini song
nodes.full: The deep polyphonic work-songs of the pearl divers, the urban sawt tradition, and the maʾtam recitation of the Shiʿi houses of mourning — the musical heritage of the two seas, part of it now on the UNESCO intangible-heritage list.
nodes.src: the UNESCO inscription of the fidjeri (2025); the Bahraini sawt and khaliji music literature.

nodes.label: The Gulf's oldest labour movement
nodes.full: Bahrain had the region's earliest and strongest workers' organisation — the strikes and uprisings of 1938, 1954–56 and 1965, the General Federation of Trade Unions — a left, cross-sectarian tradition that the sectarianisation of politics after 2011 largely broke.
nodes.src: the histories of the Bahraini labour movement; the 1965 uprising (the 'March Intifada').

nodes.label: The record and the counter-charge
nodes.full: Bahrain is among the most thoroughly documented crackdowns in the Gulf — the BICI report, the UN communications, the work of the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy — against the government's charge that this is a campaign, and the counter-charge of 'reform-washing' through the Grand Prix.
nodes.src: the BICI report and its follow-up assessments; the sportswashing analyses of the Bahrain Grand Prix.

nodes.label: The 'political naturalisation' debate
nodes.full: The long-running allegation — given weight by the leaked 2006 'Bandargate' report — that the government has naturalised tens of thousands of foreign Sunnis, many recruited into the security forces, to shift the sectarian balance of the electorate.
nodes.src: the 2006 report attributed to Ṣalāḥ al-Bandar; Gengler (2015) on the demographic-engineering claim.

nodes.label: First in, first out of oil
nodes.full: Bahrain was the first Gulf state to strike oil, at Jabal al-Dukhān in 1932, and the first to face its exhaustion. Its production is small and declining, and it depends on the shared Abū Saʿfa field with Saudi Arabia and on Saudi aid.
nodes.src: the Bahrain Petroleum Company history; the Abū Saʿfa revenue-sharing arrangement with Saudi Arabia.

nodes.label: The Gulf's first financial centre
nodes.full: After Beirut's civil war Bahrain became the offshore banking hub of the Gulf in the 1970s, and then a centre of Islamic finance and the seat of the AAOIFI standards body — a diversification forced by the early loss of oil, and later challenged by Dubai.
nodes.src: the Central Bank of Bahrain; the offshore-banking-unit regime of the 1970s.

nodes.label: Aluminium and the industrial base
nodes.full: Aluminium Bahrain (Alba), founded in 1971, is one of the world's largest single-site smelters, powered by subsidised gas — the heavy-industry leg of an economy that had to build one where the oil would not last.
nodes.src: the Alba company reports; the smelter's successive expansions to Line 6 (2019).

nodes.label: The causeway economy
nodes.full: The King Fahd Causeway from Saudi Arabia (1986) made Bahrain the Saudi weekend — alcohol, cinemas, restaurants, a laxer social code — and the Formula 1 Grand Prix (2004), the first in the Middle East, made it a sports-tourism brand.
nodes.src: the King Fahd Causeway Authority traffic data; the Bahrain International Circuit.

nodes.label: Debt and the Gulf bailout
nodes.full: Bahrain runs persistent deficits and carries the highest public debt in the GCC. A 2018 rescue package of 10 billion dollars from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait, tied to austerity and a new VAT, keeps it solvent — economic sovereignty traded for survival.
nodes.src: the October 2018 GCC support package; the IMF Article IV consultations on Bahrain; the 2019 VAT, raised to 10% in 2022.

nodes.label: Land reclamation and the vanishing coast
nodes.full: Bahrain has grown by roughly a tenth in area since the 1970s through reclamation — the artificial islands, the private waterfronts, the new financial harbour — at the cost of the fishing grounds, the seagrass and the public shore, a grievance that is environmental and class at once.
nodes.src: the studies of Bahraini land reclamation and coastal loss; the fishermen's protests over lost access.

nodes.label: The Fifth Fleet's home port
nodes.full: The US naval base at Juffair — the headquarters of the Fifth Fleet and of US Naval Forces Central Command — is the largest American installation in the Gulf and the physical anchor of the relationship that muted Western criticism of the 2011 crackdown.
nodes.src: NSA Bahrain; the US Fifth Fleet, re-established at Bahrain in 1995.

nodes.label: Bahrain and Saudi Arabia
nodes.full: The causeway, the shared oil field, the 2011 Peninsula Shield intervention, the 2011–12 proposal for a Gulf union centred on the two states, and the recurring bailouts — a dependence so complete that Bahrain is sometimes joked of as a Saudi province.
nodes.src: the 2011–12 Gulf-union proposal; the Abū Saʿfa and bailout arrangements.

nodes.label: Bahrain and the United States
nodes.full: The Fifth Fleet since 1995, major non-NATO ally status (2002), and a free-trade agreement (2006) — a security relationship Washington declined to jeopardise over the 2011 crackdown, drawing criticism that it applied a double standard.
nodes.src: the 2002 non-NATO ally designation; the US–Bahrain FTA (2006); the debate over the 2011 US response.

nodes.label: Bahrain and Iran
nodes.full: The Shah's claim to Bahrain dropped in 1971, the 1981 coup plot, the persistent Bahraini charge of Iranian direction of the Shiʿi opposition, and Tehran's recurring rhetorical claims to the island — a relationship of mutual accusation.
nodes.src: the 1970 UN mission that ended the Shah's claim; the Bahraini government's charges of Iranian involvement in 2011–17.

nodes.label: The Abraham Accords
nodes.full: Bahrain normalised relations with Israel in September 2020, the second Arab state to do so — a decision taken in step with the UAE and Saudi Arabia, deeply unpopular with the Bahraini public, and one the security state's control of dissent made possible.
nodes.src: the Abraham Accords Declaration (15 September 2020).

nodes.label: The Bahraini diaspora of dissent
nodes.full: The exiled opposition and the transnational human-rights networks — the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy in London, Americans for Democracy and Human Rights — that keep the Bahraini case in the UN and the European Parliament, the main external check left after 2016.
nodes.src: the reporting of BIRD and ADHRB (advocacy sources); the European Parliament resolutions on Bahrain.

nodes.label: The Gulf's exception and its warning
nodes.full: Bahrain is the Gulf state where the rentier bargain works least well — the oil is nearly gone, the citizen majority is politically excluded, the aid comes from Riyadh — and its uprisings of the 1990s and 2011 are studied across the region as the thing the other monarchies mean to avoid.
nodes.src: Gengler (2015); the comparative Gulf-monarchy literature.

nodes.label: 2011 as the road not taken
nodes.full: The 2011 uprising briefly opened the possibility of a constitutional monarchy negotiated between the crown prince and the opposition; the Peninsula Shield intervention and the hardline family wing closed it, and Bahrain became the Arab Spring's clearest case of a reform movement crushed by outside force.
nodes.src: the accounts of the aborted March 2011 dialogue; Toby Matthiesen, 'Sectarian Gulf' (2013).

nodes.label: A stabilised repression
nodes.full: As of the mid-2020s Bahrain is quiet — the opposition jailed or exiled, the political societies banned, the Grand Prix and the Abraham Accords providing an international face — a model of a Gulf state that survived its crisis by force and normalised the result.
nodes.src: the post-2017 assessments; the 2024 parliamentary election held with no legal opposition. This entry records the situation as of early 2026 and makes no prediction.

nodes.label: The jailed and the stateless
nodes.full: ʿAbd al-Hādī al-Khawāja, Nabeel Rajab, ʿAlī Salmān, the 'Bahrain 13', and the more than a thousand people stripped of citizenship since 2011 — the human cost of the crushing of the opposition, and the roster the transnational networks maintain.
nodes.src: the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention opinions; the citizenship-revocation tallies (advocacy sources, flagged).

nodes.label: The village and the town
nodes.full: The sectarian geography — the Shiʿi villages such as Sitra, Diraz and Bani Jamra that were the heart of both uprisings, and the Sunni towns and the reclaimed developments that were not — is a map of exclusion visible from the air.
nodes.src: the settlement geography analysed in Gengler (2015) and Matthiesen (2013).

nodes.label: Women in the movement and the backlash
nodes.full: Women were prominent in the 2011 protests, the medical response and the hunger strikes — Zaynab and Maryam al-Khawāja, Ghada Jamsheer — and the crackdown jailed and defamed them; the state's 'women's empowerment' record, a Supreme Council for Women and women judges, sits uneasily beside that.
nodes.src: the accounts of women in the 2011 movement; the Supreme Council for Women's official record.

nodes.label: The migrant workforce
nodes.full: Non-citizens are roughly half of Bahrain's population and most of its private-sector labour, under a kafala system that a 2009 reform tried briefly to soften. Migrant workers were also caught up in the 2011 crackdown, some attacked as suspected government loyalists or as bystanders.
nodes.src: the 2009 sponsorship reform and its partial reversal; the Migrant-Rights.org reporting on Bahrain.
